report:
## Conclusion

The claim that prolonged use of cloth or surgical masks causes dangerous CO2 buildup is **not supported by scientific evidence**. Multiple studies and fact-checks find that CO2 molecules are extremely small and pass through cloth and surgical mask fabric easily, escaping around the mask edges rather than accumulating to harmful levels.

Direct measurements back this up: researchers who tested CO2 levels behind masks—including with sensitive equipment—found only small, physiologically insignificant increases, far below concentrations known to cause hypercapnia (roughly >5% or 50,000 ppm for real symptoms). Viral claims that mask CO2 reaches "30,000 ppm" have been specifically debunked, since even loose readings taken by holding a monitor directly against the mouth inside a mask don't reflect what a person actually inhales (https://climatefactchecks.org/post-falsely-claims-co2-levels-reach-30000-ppm-within-face-masks/).

Reuters and BBC fact-checks reviewed viral videos and claims, consulting physiologists who confirmed CO2 diffuses through and around masks quickly, and that blood-oxygen and CO2 levels remain normal in healthy mask-wearers, including children (https://www.reuters.com/article/fact-check/covid-19-face-masks-do-not-trap-dangerous-levels-of-carbon-dioxide-idUSL1N2T01U3/, https://www.bbc.com/news/53108405). USA Today's review of clinical studies similarly found no evidence of hypoxia or hypercapnia from routine surgical or cloth mask use (https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/factcheck/2020/05/30/fact-check-wearing-face-mask-not-cause-hypoxia-hypercapnia/5260106002/).

The one caveat: N95 respirators, due to tighter sealing, can modestly raise CO2 in certain vulnerable populations (severe COPD, certain occupational settings), but this is different from cloth/surgical masks and still doesn't equate to "dangerous poisoning" for the general public.

**Bottom line:** The evidence contradicts this claim for typical cloth/surgical mask use.
